decisions.quote: Reassigning responsibility is the most prominent and best-replicated intervention against escalating commitment (i.e., the failure to withdraw from losing courses of action). This intervention is considered effective because it reduces reinvestments after negative feedback in decision scenarios with a single reinvestment decision. However, we argue that any intervention against escalating commitment should fulfill two additional criteria. The first is temporal stability, that is, the beneficial effects of the intervention need to persist beyond a single reinvestment decision. The second is specific effectiveness, that is, the intervention should reduce commitment only if the project continues to fail after an initial setback (structural failure) but not if it recovers and is ultimately profitable (temporary failure). To subject reassignment of responsibility to this critical test of effectiveness, we introduce a modification of the escalation paradigm that allows testing for temporal stability and differentiates between structural and temporary failure.
decisions.reason: The available source text (10.1037/xap0000366, Schultze & Schulz-Hardt, 2022) consists only of the title, authors, DOI, and abstract. The abstract states that the paper empirically retests the intervention of reassigning responsibility against escalating commitment across two experiments using a modified escalation paradigm. However, the abstract contains no citations, author names, publication years, titles, or DOIs for the original study or studies establishing the responsibility-reassignment intervention or escalation paradigm. Consequently, primary source evidence is insufficient to establish whether the retested original is already represented by shipped row 1509 (Staw, 1976, 'Knee-deep in the big muddy: a study of escalating commitment to a chosen course of action', DOI 10.1016/0030-5073(76)90005-2) or whether an unshipped original paper is being retested.
